processing: Light to medium oxidation with Minnan-style shaking; the rolled leaves are then pressed in a small wooden mould into a square cake, wrapped in paper and dried slowly at low heat. The roast is usually light, sometimes medium.
harvest_season: Spring (late April to May) and autumn (October), with a smaller summer picking; spring and autumn lots are the ones to buy.
appearance_dry: A small square of compressed twisted leaves, roughly 4–5 cm across and about 10 g, olive to dark green, wrapped in thin white paper.
appearance_liquor: Bright golden-yellow to light orange, clear.
appearance_wet: Long, thick, whole Shui Xian leaves that gradually free themselves from the block, olive with red edges.
taste_profile: Orchid and narcissus florals with honey and a soft, creamy sweetness, more delicate than Wuyi Shui Xian, a light roast underneath and a clean, cooling finish.

brewing.notes: One square per 150 ml pot or large gaiwan; do not break it up. Rinse once and give the first steep time: the block takes two or three infusions to loosen, and the best cups come in the middle of the session.

vintage_note: Sold by season, spring and autumn of the current year, in boxes of individually wrapped squares with the season on the box; lightly roasted lots keep a year or two at room temperature and medium-roasted ones longer. Zhangping also sells aged squares, typically three to ten years old, with the year stated.
description:
Zhangping Shui Xian is China's pressed oolong: Shui Xian leaf from the hills of Zhangping in western Fujian, moulded into little paper-wrapped squares the size of a matchbox. It is the one oolong that looks like a pu-erh cake, and the only one most drinkers will ever see in compressed form.

The story is a practical one. In the 1910s a tea maker in Shuangyang township began pressing his rolled Shui Xian into wooden moulds so it would travel and keep better, and the format stuck. The leaf is withered and shaken in the Minnan style to a light or medium oxidation, rolled, pressed into the square while still pliable, wrapped in paper and then dried slowly at low heat, which doubles as a light roast. The result is a tea that is compact, stable and oddly charming to unwrap.

It tastes like a gentler cousin of Wuyi Shui Xian: orchid and narcissus aroma, honey, a soft creamy sweetness and a light toast, with a cooling finish and none of the heavy roast or mineral grip of the rock-tea version. The cup is golden rather than amber.

Brewing is where people go wrong. Use a whole square in a 150 ml pot or a big gaiwan, do not crumble it, rinse, and be patient: the block opens over two or three steeps, so the first infusion is pale and the fourth is the best. Boiling water is fine; it does not turn bitter. Eight infusions is normal and a well-made square will go further.

It is sold by season in boxes of wrapped squares, spring and autumn, and the name is protected as a geographical indication, so look for Zhangping on the label rather than just Shui Xian. Lightly roasted lots are for this year and next; medium roasts keep, and Zhangping shops sell aged squares that turn honeyed and plummy with a few years. It is an excellent travel tea and a good gift for someone who thinks all oolong is loose leaf.
sources_note: The 1910s origin in Shuangyang township (usually dated 1914 and credited to a maker named Deng Guanjin) follows the standard local account; square size and weight vary by maker (8–12 g).
history:
Shui Xian came to Zhangping in western Fujian from the north of the province. The heritage record has a late Qing farmer of Shuangyang, Liu Yongfa, bringing seedlings from Shuiji in Jian'ou and combining northern oolong methods with local practice, with Deng Guanjin as his successor.

The square itself is usually dated to 1914 and credited to Deng, although the heritage record gives more weight to Liu, so the credit is not fully settled. The method was to wrap the rolled leaf in paper, press it in a wooden mould and dry it, which gave the local name, paper-wrapped tea.

The tea is now a geographical indication product, and its making is on the fifth batch of China's national intangible heritage list.
